headline: Browser-based OS runs AI kernel with zero install
summary: Solips-webos is a desktop environment built entirely in the browser, allowing an AI to interact with an OS using a visible cursor.
details: A new project called Solips-webos aims to push the boundaries of browser technology by creating a fully functional desktop operating system that runs entirely client-side.
The core innovation is an AI kernel that can interact with the OS, manipulating the UI like a human user would, complete with a visible cursor.
This means the AI can manage files, execute commands, and navigate the system within a secure browser environment, all without any backend servers or installation required.
Files are stored locally using IndexedDB, and the 'kernel' can be pointed to various LLMs like those from Ollama, LM Studio, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, or Grok.
The entire OS is built using static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, offering a unique approach to building browser-based operating systems and interacting with AI.
caption:
Imagine an AI controlling an operating system with a visible cursor—all within your browser.

A new project called Solips-webos aims to push the boundaries of browser technology by creating a fully functional desktop operating system that runs entirely client-side.

The core innovation is an AI kernel that can interact with the OS, manipulating the UI like a human user would, complete with a visible cursor.

This means the AI can manage files, execute commands, and navigate the system within a secure browser environment, all without any backend servers or installation required.

Files are stored locally using IndexedDB, and the 'kernel' can be pointed to various LLMs like those from Ollama, LM Studio, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, or Grok.

The entire OS is built using static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, offering a unique approach to building browser-based operating systems and interacting with AI.

headline_marked: Stop Prompting LLMs: [[Treat Them as Unreliable Functions]] for Robust Software
headline: Stop Prompting LLMs: Treat Them as Unreliable Functions for Robust Software
summary: Developers often treat LLMs as magic boxes, but their probabilistic nature demands a validation layer. Learn how to build reliable software around AI's inherent unpredictability.
details: Many developers start with AI by writing a long prompt and hoping for a valid JSON output, but the 20% failure rate in production can be disastrous, leading to runtime errors and debugging nightmares. Treating LLMs as magic boxes instead of software components is a common pitfall.

LLMs are probabilistic, not deterministic. Even with temperature set to zero, you cannot guarantee consistent output formats across different model versions or high-load periods. Assuming the AI will always return a specific key in a JSON object makes your code fragile, akin to calling a function that might change its return type without warning.

Instead of trusting the output, build a validation layer between the LLM and your business logic. Treat LLM output as 'untrusted user input.' Define a strict schema using libraries like Zod or Pydantic to validate the response immediately. If validation fails, prevent the data from reaching your database or frontend.

Implement a retry loop with a fallback mechanism. If the LLM returns a malformed response, send the error message back to the LLM and ask it to fix the specific formatting error. This is far more effective than simply retrying the same prompt multiple times.

A key mistake is asking the AI to 'describe' something, as descriptions are variable. Instead, force the AI to choose from a predefined list of enums. For example, instead of 'Categorize this feedback as positive, negative, or neutral,' use 'Categorize this feedback. You must choose exactly one value from this list: [POSITIVE, NEGATIVE, NEUTRAL]. Do not include any other text in your response.'

To measure prompt effectiveness, create a golden dataset of 50-100 input/output examples. Run this dataset through the model every time you change a prompt. This turns prompt engineering into a measurable process, providing a percentage accuracy score instead of relying on guesswork.

The core principle is to stop trying to write the perfect prompt, which does not exist. Instead, build a system that anticipates AI failures. By treating the LLM as an unreliable function, you can construct reliable software around it.
